grammar.explanation:
~(으)면 joins two clauses. The first is a condition; the second says what happens once it is met. English says "if" or "when" depending on how sure the condition is. Use it for plans, suggestions and instructions.

If the stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ, add ~면: 오다 → 오 + 면 → 오면; 살다 → 살 + 면 → 살면. If it ends in a consonant, add ~으면: 있다 → 있 + 으면 → 있으면; 먹다 → 먹 + 으면 → 먹으면. Nouns use 이다: 학생 → 학생이면; 의사 → 의사면.

Irregulars change as usual before 으: ㅂ becomes 우 (춥다 → 추우면), ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 → 들으면), ㅅ drops (낫다 → 나으면), and ㅎ drops (그렇다 → 그러면). ㄹ stems never add 으: 만들다 → 만들면, not 만들으면.

For a future condition, ~(으)면 stays in its basic form: 내일 비가 오면 ... The future tense goes only on the final verb (안 할 거예요).

examples.ko: 비가 오면 빨래를 안 할 거예요.
examples.en: If it rains, I won't do the laundry.

examples.ko: 내일 시간이 있으면 같이 영화를 봐요.
examples.en: If you have time tomorrow, let's watch a movie.
When the signal changes, cross the street.
If the weather is cold, I will stay home.
When class finishes, please call me.

examples.ko: 이 노래를 들으면 그 사람이 생각날 거예요.
examples.en: If you listen to this song, you will think of that person.
examples.note: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣 + 으면 → 들으면.

examples.en: If you are a student, the ticket is cheap.

grammar.explanation:
The same ending can state a general truth or a habit: every time A happens, B happens. 겨울이 되면 날씨가 추워져요 is true every year, not just once. "Whenever" or "every time" is often the best English translation.

Because these are repeated facts rather than one-off future events, the final verb is normally in the present tense, not ~ㄹ/을 거예요. Compare 피곤하면 커피를 마셔요 (whenever I'm tired, I drink coffee: a habit) with 피곤하면 커피를 마실 거예요 (if I'm tired later, I'll drink coffee: one occasion).

Formation is the same as before: 되다 → 되면; 높다 → 높으면; 덥다 → 더우면. The result often uses ~아/어지다 (to become), as in 추워져요.

examples.en: When winter comes, the weather gets cold.

examples.ko: 습도가 높으면 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
examples.en: When the humidity is high, laundry doesn't dry well.
Whenever I am tired, I drink coffee.

examples.ko: 콜라를 많이 마시면 잠을 잘 못 자요.
examples.en: If I drink a lot of cola, I can't sleep well.
When spring comes, lots of flowers bloom.
Whenever I get stressed, I eat a lot.
When the weather is hot, people go to the sea.
examples.note: 덥다 is ㅂ irregular: 더 + 우면 → 더우면.

grammar.explanation:
Use this to imagine a past that did not happen and say what the result would have been: "if I had..., I would have...". It often expresses regret or relief.

Build the condition with the past tense + ~으면. The past marker ends in ㅆ, so it always takes ~으면: 자다 → 잤 + 으면 → 잤으면; 먹다 → 먹었 + 으면 → 먹었으면; 공부하다 → 공부했으면. Nouns: 학생이었으면, 의사였으면.

Build the result with the past tense + ~을 거예요: 가다 → 갔 + 을 거예요 → 갔을 거예요; 좋다 → 좋았을 거예요. For a negative result use ~지 않았을 거예요. Even when the result is about now ("I wouldn't be tired today"), Korean keeps it in this past form.

~았/었더라면 can replace ~았/었으면 with the same meaning and sounds a little more emphatic.

examples.ko: 어제 일찍 잤으면 오늘 피곤하지 않았을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had slept early yesterday, I wouldn't be tired today.

examples.ko: 우산이 있었으면 비를 맞지 않았을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had had an umbrella, I wouldn't have gotten rained on.

examples.ko: 그 남자가 수상하지 않았으면 문을 열었을 거예요.
examples.en: If that man hadn't been suspicious, I would have opened the door.

examples.ko: 조금 더 빨리 왔으면 버스를 탔을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had come a bit earlier, I would have caught the bus.
examples.note: 오다 → 왔다 → 왔으면: the past marker always takes ~으면.

examples.en: If the weather had been nice, I would have gone to the park.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 의사였으면 저를 도와줬을 거예요.
examples.en: If that person had been a doctor, they would have helped me.

grammar.explanation:
~ㄴ/는다면 means "if", like ~(으)면, but it stresses that the condition is only a supposition: something imagined, unlikely, or not yet known. It suits daydreams ("if I were rich") and "if it's true that...".

Form it in two steps: put the word in the plain (diary) form from Lesson 5, then add ~면. Vowel verbs: 가다 → 간다 → 간다면. Consonant verbs: 먹다 → 먹는다 → 먹는다면. ㄹ stems drop ㄹ: 살다 → 산다 → 산다면. Adjectives just add ~다면: 좋다 → 좋다면. Past: 갔다 → 갔다면. Nouns: 학생이라면, and after a vowel 의사라면 or 너라면.

Compare 비가 오면 (a neutral "if/when it rains") with 비가 온다면 ("suppose it rains"). For pure imagination such as "if I were you", ~ㄴ/는다면 or ~(이)라면 is the natural choice.

examples.ko: 내일 날씨가 좋다면 공원에 갈 거예요.
examples.en: If the weather is nice tomorrow, I'll go to the park.

examples.ko: 제가 과학자가 된다면 습도를 연구하고 싶어요.
examples.en: If I became a scientist, I would want to study humidity.

examples.ko: 돈이 많다면 큰 집을 살 거예요.
examples.en: If I had a lot of money, I would buy a big house.

examples.ko: 내가 너라면 그 사람을 믿지 않을 거야.
examples.en: If I were you, I wouldn't trust that person.

examples.ko: 매일 채소를 먹는다면 더 건강해질 거예요.
examples.en: If you ate vegetables every day, you would get healthier.

examples.ko: 한국에 산다면 매일 김치를 먹을 거예요.
examples.en: If I lived in Korea, I would eat kimchi every day.
examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ in the plain form: 산다 → 산다면.

examples.en: If that is true, it is a big problem.

grammar.explanation:
만약 goes at the start of a conditional sentence. It adds no meaning of its own; it just tells the listener early that an "if" is coming, a bit like "suppose" or "in case".

It does not make a sentence conditional by itself. You still need a conditional ending later: 만약 ... ~(으)면, ~ㄴ/는다면 or ~았/었으면. 만약 비가 와요 is wrong; say 만약 비가 오면.

It is optional, and most useful in long sentences where the ~면 comes late. 만약에 is a common spoken variant with the same meaning.

examples.ko: 만약 내일 비바람이 치면 경기가 취소될 거예요.
examples.en: If there is a rainstorm tomorrow, the game will be cancelled.
If I am late, go ahead first.

examples.ko: 만약 돈이 있었으면 그 집을 샀을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had had money, I would have bought that house.

examples.ko: 만약 그 사람이 전화하면 저한테 알려 주세요.
examples.en: If that person calls, please let me know.
If you get lost, ask a police officer.
examples.note: 만약에 means the same as 만약.

examples.ko: 만약 제가 부자라면 세계 여행을 할 거예요.
examples.en: If I were rich, I would travel around the world.

grammar.explanation:
These are ready-made linking words that start a sentence and react to what was just said.

그러면 is 그렇다 + ~으면. 그렇다 is ㅎ irregular, so ㅎ drops: 그렇 + 으면 → 그러면. It means "then" or "in that case". In speech it is often shortened to 그럼.

그렇다면 is 그렇다 + ~다면, the supposition form. It means "if that's so" and sounds a little more careful than 그러면.

아니면 is 아니다 + ~면: "if not" or "otherwise". Between two nouns or two options it means "or" when offering a choice (커피 아니면 콜라). Don't use 하고 or 와/과 for this; they mean "and".

examples.en: In that case, let's meet tomorrow.
If so, I won't go either.

examples.ko: 빨리 진정하세요. 아니면 콜라를 안 줄 거예요.
examples.en: Calm down quickly. Otherwise I won't give you a cola.

examples.ko: 저는 커피 아니면 콜라를 마시고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to drink coffee or cola.
Are you busy? Then let's talk later.
Then come again next week.
examples.note: 그럼 is the short spoken form of 그러면.

examples.ko: 오늘 갈 거예요, 아니면 내일 갈 거예요?
examples.en: Are you going today, or tomorrow?

vocab.en: to back out on, to betray
to turn on (music, TV, tap, AC)
to write up, to fill out

grammar.explanation:
~자 is the casual way to say "let's...". Use it with close friends, siblings, or people younger than you. It is 반말, so it cannot take ~요 (먹자요 is wrong).

Add ~자 straight to any verb stem. Vowel or consonant doesn't matter, and irregular verbs don't change: 가다 → 가자; 먹다 → 먹자; 듣다 → 듣자; 만들다 → 만들자.

For "let's not", combine ~지 말다 (from the negative command) with ~자: 보다 → 보지 말자.

Only verbs take ~자. You can't suggest being an adjective, so 좋자 or 행복하자 don't work as "let's".

examples.en: Let's eat together.
Let's rest at home today.
Let's not watch that movie.
Let's memorize these words together.
Let's meet again tomorrow.
Let's listen to music together.
examples.note: No irregular change before ~자: 듣 + 자 → 듣자.

examples.en: Let's make a cake on the weekend.

grammar.explanation:
~ㅂ/읍시다 also means "let's...", but it is more formal than ~자. You hear it in meetings, at work, in speeches and on signs, and between adults who aren't close. A boss uses it with a team.

After a vowel, add ㅂ under the last syllable plus 시다: 가다 → 갑시다; 하다 → 합시다; 쉬다 → 쉽시다. After a consonant, add ~읍시다: 먹다 → 먹읍시다; 앉다 → 앉읍시다. ㄹ stems drop ㄹ and add ~ㅂ시다: 만들다 → 만듭시다. ㄷ irregulars change ㄷ to ㄹ: 걷다 → 걸읍시다.

For "let's not", use ~지 맙시다: 가지 맙시다.

Despite the 시, it is not honorific. Said to a boss or an older person it can sound like an order. With seniors, ask with ~(으)실래요? instead.

examples.en: Let's start the meeting.
Let's take a short rest here.
Let's fill out this document today.
Let's recruit new employees next month.
Let's have lunch together.
Let's not make phone calls during the meeting.
Let's walk to the park.
examples.note: 걷다 is ㄷ irregular: 걷 → 걸 + 읍시다.

grammar.point: ~ㄹ/을래요?: shall we? / do you want to?
grammar.explanation:
As a question, ~ㄹ/을래요? asks what the listener wants to do. It is a friendly way to invite someone ("shall we...?") or ask their preference ("what do you want to...?").

After a vowel add ~ㄹ래요: 가다 → 갈래요; 마시다 → 마실래요. After a consonant add ~을래요: 먹다 → 먹을래요; 앉다 → 앉을래요. ㄹ stems just add 래요: 만들다 → 만들래요. Irregulars change before 으: 듣다 → 들을래요; 돕다 → 도울래요. Drop ~요 with friends: 갈래?

To be extra polite, add honorific ~(으)시: 가실래요?, 드실래요? (from 드시다).

It works only with verbs and asks about the listener's will. Said with 맞다 or 혼나다 (맞을래?), it becomes an annoyed, empty threat: "do you want to get hit?"

examples.en: Shall we have coffee together?
What do you want to do on the weekend?
Do you want to watch a movie tonight?
Do you want to sit here?
Would you like some coffee?
examples.note: 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다/마시다, so this is extra polite.

examples.en: Do you want to listen to a song together?

grammar.explanation:
~아/어 줄래요? literally asks "do you want to do it for me?", which works as a soft request: "could you...?". It sounds gentler than a command like ~아/어 주세요, because it asks rather than tells.

Put the verb in its ~아/어 form, add 주다, then put ~ㄹ래요 on 주다: 열다 → 열어 → 열어 줄래요?; 하다 → 해 → 해 줄래요?; 기다리다 → 기다려 → 기다려 줄래요? With just a thing and no verb, use 주다 alone: 물 좀 줄래요?

For someone older or senior, make 주다 honorific: ~아/어 주실래요? With friends, drop 요: 해 줄래? Adding 좀 softens it further, much like "please".

examples.en: Could you open the door?
Can you turn on some music?
Could you please give this note to the teacher?
Could you give me some water?
Could you wait just a moment?
examples.note: 기다리 + 어 contracts to 기다려.

examples.en: Can you help me with this?
examples.note: 돕다 is ㅂ irregular: 돕 + 아 → 도와.

grammar.explanation:
Without a question, ~ㄹ/을래요 tells people what you want to do or have just decided to do: "I'll..." or "I want to...". It is very common when ordering food or choosing between options.

It is formed exactly like the question: 가다 → 갈래요; 먹다 → 먹을래요; 쉬다 → 쉴래요; 만들다 → 만들래요; 듣다 → 들을래요.

How it differs: ~고 싶어요 is a wish ("I'd like to"); ~ㄹ/을 거예요 is a plan or prediction; ~ㄹ/을래요 is your choice right now, based on what you feel like. It only expresses the speaker's own will, so don't use it for other people's plans.

For "I don't want to", put 안 before the verb (안 갈래요) or use ~지 않을래요.

examples.en: I'll have bibimbap.
I want to rest at home today.
I don't want to go.
I'll have water.
I'll sit at the back.
I don't want to do anything today.

vocab.en: to occur, to come up, to arise
to step aside, to step away

grammar.explanation:
~ㄹ/을 수 있다 means "can": someone is able to do something, or something is possible. 수 is a noun meaning roughly "way", so the idea is "there is a way to do it".

Put the verb in the future modifier form (Lesson 26), then add 수 있다. After a vowel add ~ㄹ: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요; 하다 → 할 수 있어요. After a consonant add ~을: 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. ㄹ stems keep their ㄹ: 만들다 → 만들 수 있어요. Irregulars change before 으: 걷다 → 걸을 수 있어요; 돕다 → 도울 수 있어요.

It covers ability ("I can swim") and possibility ("you can use this book"). As a question, often with ~아/어 주다 and 좀, it becomes a polite request: 좀 비켜 줄 수 있어요?

examples.ko: 저는 한국어를 유창하게 말할 수 있어요.
examples.en: I can speak Korean fluently.

examples.ko: 이 서류를 내일까지 작성할 수 있어요?
examples.en: Can you fill out this form by tomorrow?
Could you step aside a little?
You can refer to this book.

examples.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 있어요.
examples.en: I can eat spicy food.
I can make kimchi stew.
examples.note: ㄹ stems add nothing: 만들 + 수 있어요.

examples.en: Can I take the bus from here?

grammar.explanation:
Replace 있다 with 없다 to say something is impossible: "cannot". The first part is formed the same way: 가다 → 갈 수 없어요; 먹다 → 먹을 수 없어요; 걷다 → 걸을 수 없어요.

You now know three ways to say "can't": 못 + verb (못 가요), ~지 못하다 (가지 못해요) from Lesson 20, and ~ㄹ/을 수 없다. They overlap a lot. 못 is the most common in casual talk; ~ㄹ/을 수 없다 sounds a little more objective, as if the situation makes it impossible.

Some verbs carry a nuance: 이해할 수 없다 suggests something you fundamentally cannot understand or accept, while 이해 못 하겠다 is more "I'm not getting it right now".

Don't confuse it with 안. 안 가요 means you choose not to go; 갈 수 없어요 means you are unable to.

examples.ko: 길이 미끄러워서 빨리 걸을 수 없어요.
examples.en: The road is slippery so I can't walk fast.

examples.ko: 기한이 지나서 환불을 받을 수 없어요.
examples.en: The deadline has passed so you can't get a refund.

examples.ko: 저는 그 사람의 행동을 이해할 수 없어요.
examples.en: I can't understand that person's behavior.
I'm busy today, so I can't meet.

examples.ko: 이 음식은 너무 매워서 먹을 수 없어요.
examples.en: This food is too spicy, so I can't eat it.
Why can't you come?

grammar.explanation:
The ~ㄹ/을 수 part never changes. To show tense, conjugate only the final 있다 or 없다.

Present: 갈 수 있어요 / 갈 수 없어요. Past: 갈 수 있었어요 (I could, I was able to) / 갈 수 없었어요 (I couldn't). Future or guess: 갈 수 있을 거예요 (I'll probably be able to) / 갈 수 없을 거예요.

A common mistake is putting the past on the main verb. 갔을 수 있어요 is a different pattern meaning "might have gone", not "was able to go". Keep the main verb in its ~ㄹ/을 form and put the tense at the end.

examples.ko: 어제는 일이 많아서 잘 수 없었어요.
examples.en: I couldn't sleep yesterday because I had a lot of work.
I will probably be able to go tomorrow.
I could swim when I was young.
Back then I couldn't read Korean.

examples.ko: 다음 주에는 만날 수 없을 거예요.
examples.en: I probably won't be able to meet next week.
Were you able to sleep yesterday?

grammar.explanation:
Because 수 is a noun, particles can attach to it like any other noun. Adding ~가 (수가 있다/없다) keeps the meaning but adds emphasis. 수가 없다 often sounds like "just can't, no matter what", and is common when complaining or explaining something frustrating.

Put 가 right after 수 with no space: 갈 수 없어요 → 갈 수가 없어요; 참을 수 없어요 → 참을 수가 없어요. Tense still goes on the final word: 잘 수가 없었어요.

수가 없다 is much more common than 수가 있다. The nuances of 수는 and 수도 come in later lessons.

examples.ko: 너무 웃겨서 웃음을 참을 수가 없어요.
examples.en: It's so funny I just can't hold back my laughter.
I really can't go right now.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 혼자 풀 수가 없어요.
examples.en: I just can't solve this problem alone.
It was so noisy I just couldn't sleep.

examples.ko: 그 사람 말을 믿을 수가 없어요.
examples.en: I just can't believe what that person says.

lessons.title: Lesson 46: I have to/I need to ~아/어야 하다/되다/지/겠다, ~ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다

grammar.explanation:
~아/어야 하다 (or ~아/어야 되다) says something is necessary. One Korean form covers English "must", "have to" and "should", so context and tone decide how strong it is.

Start from the ~아/어 form you know from ~아/어요, add ~야, then 하다 or 되다. ㅏ/ㅗ stems take ~아야: 가다 → 가 + 아야 → 가야 해요; 보다 → 보 + 아야 → 봐야 해요. Other stems take ~어야: 먹다 → 먹어야 해요; 마시다 → 마셔야 해요. 하다 words take ~해야: 공부하다 → 공부해야 해요. Irregulars follow their usual ~아/어 form: 듣다 → 들어야, 돕다 → 도와야, 쓰다 → 써야.

하다 and 되다 mean the same here; 돼요 is more common in speech. Only the last word changes for tense: 가야 했어요 (had to), 가야 할 거예요 (will have to).

"Don't have to" is a different pattern (Lesson 49); simply adding 안 does not give that meaning.

examples.en: I have to review this document by tomorrow.

examples.ko: 대학교에 가고 싶으면 열심히 공부해야 돼요.
examples.en: If you want to go to university, you should study hard.
I had to work late yesterday.
We will have to leave in 10 minutes.
I have to get up early tomorrow morning.
I have to take medicine today.
You should listen carefully to the teacher.
examples.note: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣 + 어야 → 들어야.

grammar.explanation:
In conversation, the final 하다/되다 is often replaced with ~지, or ~죠 (short for ~지요) to be polite: 가야 해요 → 가야죠. It attaches directly to ~아/어야 with no space.

It sounds natural and a little emotional: "of course I/you should", "I really ought to". About yourself, it sounds like a reminder or a decision. To someone else, it is gentle advice or a push.

Form ~아/어야 as usual, then add ~지/죠: 가다 → 가야지; 먹다 → 먹어야지; 하다 → 해야지; 자다 → 자야죠. Use ~지 with friends and ~죠 where you would use ~요.

examples.en: I should go home now.
If you're sick, you should take medicine.
You should exercise every day.
The exam is tomorrow? Then you should study today.
It's twelve o'clock? I should go to bed now.
When guests come, you should treat them well.

grammar.explanation:
~아/어야겠다 is short for ~아/어야 하겠다. It combines "must" with ~겠 (intention or guess), so it sounds like "I guess I'd better..." or "I think I should...". The speaker has just noticed something and makes a decision on the spot.

Make ~아/어야 as usual, then add ~겠어요: 가다 → 가야겠어요; 먹다 → 먹어야겠어요; 하다 → 해야겠어요; 쉬다 → 쉬어야겠어요.

Compare: 가야 해요 states an obligation ("I have to go"); 가야겠어요 is a decision you just reached ("I'd better go"). That is why it is usually about the speaker, and why a reason with ~아/어서 often comes first: 늦어서 가야겠어요.

examples.en: It's late, so I'd better go now.
My eyesight got worse, so I guess I'll have to buy glasses.
I'd better get up earlier next time.
I'm hungry, so I'd better eat something.
examples.note: 고프다 drops ㅡ: 고프 + 아서 → 고파서.

examples.en: I have a headache, so I'd better rest early today.
I guess I'd better take an umbrella tomorrow.

grammar.explanation:
필요하다 means "to be necessary", and it is how you say you need something. In English "need" takes an object, but 필요하다 is an adjective, so the needed thing is the subject and takes ~이/가, not ~을/를.

Think of it as "for me, X is necessary": 저는 돈이 필요해요 = "I need money". Use 이 after a consonant (돈이) and 가 after a vowel (우유가). A common mistake is 돈을 필요해요.

필요 없어요 ("not needed", "I don't need it") is very common. To say you need to do something, use ~아/어야 하다 or ~ㄹ/을 필요가 있다 (next point).

examples.en: I need a new photocopier.
This work needs everyone's cooperation.
Do you need more time?
I need some milk.
I don't need money.
I needed help back then.

grammar.point: ~ㄹ/을 필요가 있다/없다: need to / don't need to
grammar.explanation:
필요 is the noun "necessity". Describe it with a verb in the ~ㄹ/을 future modifier form, then add 있다 ("there is a need to") or 없다 ("there is no need to").

After a vowel add ~ㄹ: 가다 → 갈 필요가 있어요; 사다 → 살 필요가 없어요. After a consonant add ~을: 먹다 → 먹을 필요가 없어요. ㄹ stems keep ㄹ: 만들다 → 만들 필요가 없어요.

필요가 있다 is close to ~아/어야 하다 but softer and a bit more formal. The 없다 version is the more useful one: a natural way to say "you don't need to". Tense goes on 있다/없다: 갈 필요가 없었어요.

examples.ko: 이 문제를 다시 검토할 필요가 있어요.
examples.en: We need to look at this problem again.
There's no need to worry.
You don't need to come early tomorrow.
You don't need to buy that book.
Do we need to make it again?
I didn't need to get up early yesterday.

vocab.en: to stick out, to hold out

grammar.explanation:
~지만 means "but" or "even though". It joins two clauses that contrast: A, but B. Use it when the second fact goes against what the first would suggest.

Add ~지만 directly to the stem. Nothing changes, vowel or consonant, and irregulars stay as they are: 작다 → 작지만; 바쁘다 → 바쁘지만; 어렵다 → 어렵지만. Nouns use 이다: 학생이지만; after a vowel 이 is often dropped (의사지만).

For tense, put the past or future before ~지만: 갔지만 (went, but); 가겠지만 or 갈 거지만 (will go, but).

The first clause is a fact the speaker accepts. That separates it from ~아/어도 (Lesson 48), where the first clause is only a possibility: 비가 오지만 = it is raining, but; 비가 와도 = even if it rains. 죄송하지만 ("I'm sorry, but") is a common way to soften a request.

examples.en: This apartment is small but clean.
I like animals, but I can't raise one.
I was very sick, but I took part in the match.

examples.ko: 내일 비가 오겠지만 저는 갈 거예요.
examples.en: It will probably rain tomorrow, but I will go.
Korean is difficult but fun.
examples.note: 어렵다 is ㅂ irregular, but ~지만 causes no change.

examples.en: My older brother is a student, but he works too.
I'm sorry, but I can't call right now.

grammar.explanation:
그렇지만 is 그렇다 ("to be so") + ~지만, literally "it is so, but". It starts a new sentence and means "however" or "but even so", contrasting with the sentence before.

It is the same idea as ~지만, split into two sentences: 비싸지만 좋아요 = 비싸요. 그렇지만 좋아요. ~지만 doesn't affect the ㅎ: 그렇 + 지만 → 그렇지만.

하지만 is the most common sentence-starting "but" in everyday speech. 그렇지만 means the same and sounds slightly more formal or careful.

examples.en: However, I don't have time now.
Even so, I trust that person.

examples.ko: 그렇지만 차가 너무 커서 주차할 수 없어요.
examples.en: However, the car is too big, so I can't park it.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 비싸요. 그렇지만 음식이 정말 맛있어요.
examples.en: That restaurant is expensive. But the food is really delicious.

examples.ko: 저도 가고 싶어요. 그렇지만 내일 시험이 있어요.
examples.en: I want to go too. However, I have an exam tomorrow.

grammar.explanation:
~아/어도 means "even if" or "even though": the second clause holds no matter what happens in the first. It is the ~아/어 form you know from ~아/어요, plus ~도 ("also, even").

ㅏ/ㅗ stems take ~아도: 가다 → 가 + 아도 → 가도; 보다 → 보 + 아도 → 봐도. Other stems take ~어도: 먹다 → 먹어도; 마시다 → 마셔도. 하다 becomes 해도: 피곤하다 → 피곤해도. Irregulars follow their ~아/어요 form: 춥다 → 추워도; 바쁘다 → 바빠도; 듣다 → 들어도.

Compare with ~지만, which links two facts: 비가 오지만 = it's raining, but. ~아/어도 says the first part doesn't matter, real or not: 비가 와도 = even if it rains. And unlike ~(으)면 (if it rains, then...), the result does not depend on the condition.

examples.en: Even if it rains, we will play the game.
Even if you're tired, you have to do your homework.
Even if it's half price, I won't buy it.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 많이 먹어도 살이 안 쪄요.
examples.en: Even if that person eats a lot, they don't gain weight.
Even when the weather is cold, I exercise every day.
examples.note: 춥다 is ㅂ irregular: 추 + 워도 → 추워도.

examples.en: Even when I am busy, I study Korean every day.
examples.note: 바쁘다 drops ㅡ: 바쁘 + 아도 → 바빠도.

examples.en: This movie is fun even if you watch it again.

grammar.explanation:
Because the ~아/어도 clause is hypothetical, it can contain a question word, which gives "-ever" meanings: 누가 와도 (whoever comes), 어디에 가도 (wherever you go), 뭘 해도 (whatever you do), 언제 가도 (whenever you go).

아무리 + ~아/어도 means "no matter how (much)": 아무리 바빠도 (no matter how busy), 아무리 먹어도 (no matter how much I eat). 아무리 takes the place of 얼마나 here; 얼마나 바빠도 is wrong.

The second clause says what stays the same despite everything, often a negative or a firm statement: 아무리 공부해도 이해할 수 없어요.

examples.en: No matter how busy you are, you have to eat.
No matter how much I study, I can't understand it.
Don't open the door, no matter who comes.
Wherever you go, there are a lot of people.
Whenever I call, they don't answer.
Whatever I eat, it tastes good.

grammar.explanation:
With a noun, ~아/어도 attaches to 이다, which gives two forms with the same meaning: ~이어도 and ~이라도. After a consonant use them in full: 주말 → 주말이어도 / 주말이라도. After a vowel they shorten: 친구 → 친구여도 / 친구라도.

~이라도 is more common in speech. It also has another meaning ("at least, even just") that comes later, so focus on "even if it's N" for now.

For "even if it's not N", use 아니다: 학생이 아니어도 ("even if you aren't a student").

examples.en: Even on weekends, I get up early.
Even if you are a student, you must follow the rules.
Even if you're the youngest, you have to do a lot of work.
Even if you're my friend, I can't lend you money.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel, so 이어도 shortens to 여도.

examples.ko: 학생이 아니어도 이 도서관을 쓸 수 있어요.
examples.en: Even if you aren't a student, you can use this library.

grammar.explanation:
그래도 comes from 그렇다 + ~어도. 그렇다 is ㅎ irregular, so 그렇 + 어도 → 그래도, just like 그래요. It starts a sentence and means "even so", "still" or "but still".

Use it to say your point holds despite what was just said: 비가 와요. 그래도 갈 거예요. It is the sentence-starting version of ~아/어도, just as 그렇지만 is for ~지만.

Compare: 그렇지만 simply contrasts two facts ("however"). 그래도 stresses that the situation doesn't change things ("still, even so").

examples.en: Even so, I am going.
Still, you have to do your homework.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와요. 그래도 나가고 싶어요.
examples.en: It's raining a lot. Even so, I want to go out.
It's very expensive. Even so, I want to buy it.

examples.ko: 조금 아파요. 그래도 학교에 가야 돼요.
examples.en: I'm a bit sick. Still, I have to go to school.

lessons.title: Lesson 49: There is no problem if: ~아/어도 되다

grammar.point: 되다: to work, to be OK, to be done
grammar.explanation:
You know 되다 as "to become". In everyday speech it has more meanings: something works or functions (컴퓨터가 잘 돼요), something is possible or fine (내일은 돼요, "tomorrow works"), or something is done or ready (준비가 다 됐어요).

되다 + ~어요 → 되어요, usually shortened to 돼요. Past: 됐어요. 돼 is the contraction of 되어, so write 돼요, not 되요.

To say something isn't working or isn't possible, use 안 되다, not 못: 안 돼요. On its own, 안 돼! is a common "No!" or "You can't!".

됐어요 can also mean "that's enough" or "no thanks", for example when someone offers more food.

examples.en: The computer isn't working well.
Dinner is all ready.
Tomorrow doesn't work for me.
That's enough. Please stop.
Is the internet not working?
Is your homework all done?
No! Don't go in there.

grammar.explanation:
Combining ~아/어도 with 되다 literally means "even if you do it, it works out", that is, it's fine. As a question it asks permission ("May I...?"). As a statement it gives permission ("You may...").

Make ~아/어도 as in Lesson 48, then add 되다 (usually 돼요): 앉다 → 앉아도 돼요; 가다 → 가도 돼요; 먹다 → 먹어도 돼요; 하다 → 해도 돼요; 듣다 → 들어도 돼요; 쓰다 → 써도 돼요.

To answer, say 네, 돼요 or 네, ~아/어도 돼요 (yes, you may), or 아니요, 안 돼요 (no, you can't). Tense goes on 되다: 해도 될 거예요 ("it'll probably be fine").

~ㄹ/을 수 있다 is mainly about ability; ~아/어도 되다 is the natural way to ask for or give permission.

examples.en: May I sit here?
You may go home now.
Is it OK to take a picture?

examples.ko: 그 책은 내일 줘도 될 거예요.
examples.en: It will probably be fine to give me that book tomorrow.
May I use this computer?
examples.note: 쓰다 drops ㅡ: 쓰 + 어도 → 써도.

examples.en: Is it OK if I listen to music?
You can wait here.

grammar.explanation:
Put 안 before the verb, or use ~지 않아도, and the pattern means "it's fine not to": "you don't have to" or "you don't need to". It is a polite way to release someone from an obligation.

가다 → 안 가도 돼요 or 가지 않아도 돼요; 하다 → 안 해도 돼요. With noun + 하다 verbs, 안 goes right before 하다: 걱정하다 → 걱정 안 해도 돼요.

This is the natural opposite of ~아/어야 하다 (Lesson 46): 가야 해요 (you have to go) vs 안 가도 돼요 (you don't have to go). 안 가야 해요 does not mean this. ~ㄹ/을 필요가 없다 is similar but a little more formal.

examples.en: You don't have to go to school tomorrow.
You don't have to pay.
You don't have to worry.
You don't have to cook today.
You don't have to buy a present.
Is it OK if I don't come early tomorrow?

grammar.explanation:
Instead of 되다, you can finish ~아/어도 with 괜찮다 ("to be fine") or 좋다 ("to be good"). The meaning stays "it's OK if...", but the tone shifts.

~아/어도 괜찮아요? sounds softer and more considerate, good for polite questions to strangers or seniors. ~아/어도 좋아요 often sounds like warm permission ("feel free to"). ~아/어도 돼요 is the most neutral and most common.

Formation is the same: 열다 → 열어도 괜찮아요; 가다 → 가도 좋아요. The negative works too: 안 와도 괜찮아요 ("it's fine if you don't come").

examples.en: Is it all right if I open the window?
Is it okay if I call now?
You can leave work early today.
Is it all right if I sit in this chair?
It's fine if you don't come tomorrow.
Feel free to speak casually with me.

grammar.explanation:
예정 means a schedule or arranged plan. ~ㄹ/을 예정이다 says something is scheduled or expected: "be scheduled to", "be due to". It sounds a bit formal and is common in announcements, news and work talk.

Use the future modifier ~ㄹ/을 + 예정 + 이다: 가다 → 갈 예정이에요; 시작하다 → 시작할 예정이에요; 먹다 → 먹을 예정이에요. ㄹ stems keep ㄹ: 열다 → 열 예정이에요. Irregulars change before 을: 짓다 → 지을 예정이에요.

Compare with ~ㄹ/을 거예요: 갈 거예요 is a simple "will go"; 갈 예정이에요 adds that it is fixed in a schedule. The past, 갈 예정이었어요, means it was scheduled, often hinting that it didn't happen.

examples.ko: 저는 다음 달에 한국에 갈 예정이에요.
examples.en: I am scheduled to go to Korea next month.
The meeting is scheduled to start at three.

examples.ko: 그 섬에 대규모 호텔을 지을 예정이에요.
examples.en: They plan to build a large-scale hotel on that island.

examples.ko: 새 가게는 다음 주에 열 예정이에요.
examples.en: The new shop is scheduled to open next week.
What time is the plane due to arrive?
I was supposed to leave yesterday.

grammar.explanation:
계획 means "plan". ~ㄹ/을 계획이 있다 is like English "have plans to", and ~ㄹ/을 계획이 없다 is "have no plans to". ~ㄹ/을 계획이다 ("it's my plan to") is also used.

Form it like 예정: 가다 → 갈 계획이 있어요; 뽑다 → 뽑을 계획이 있어요; 살다 → 살 계획이 있어요 (ㄹ stem).

예정 is about something already scheduled, often official. 계획 is about your intention, which may still change. ~ㄹ/을 계획이 있어요? is a polite way to ask about someone's plans.

examples.ko: 저는 내년에 일을 그만둘 계획이 있어요.
examples.en: I have plans to quit my job next year.
Do you have plans to go to an island this summer?
I have no plans to get married.
I have plans to live in Korea.
I plan to buy a car this year.
examples.note: 살 here comes from 사다 (to buy), not 살다 (to live).

examples.ko: 그 회사는 사람을 더 뽑을 계획이 없어요.
examples.en: That company has no plans to hire more people.

grammar.explanation:
준비 means "preparation". ~ㄹ/을 준비가 되다 literally says "the preparation to do it is done", that is, "be ready to". Here 되다 has the "done" meaning from Lesson 49.

Verb + ~ㄹ/을 + 준비가 + 되다: 가다 → 갈 준비가 됐어요; 먹다 → 먹을 준비가 됐어요; 시작하다 → 시작할 준비가 됐어요. Without a verb, 준비가 됐어요 just means "I'm ready".

It is usually in the past tense, 됐어요, because the preparation has been completed: "is ready". 안 됐어요 or 아직 안 됐어요 means "not ready (yet)".

examples.en: I am ready to go now.
Are you ready to take the Korean SAT?
I am not ready to present yet.
Everything is ready to eat now.
Is everyone ready to leave?

grammar.explanation:
With the active verb 하다, 준비 becomes the object, so it takes ~를. ~ㄹ/을 준비를 하다 means "get ready to" or "prepare to". It describes the action of preparing, while 준비가 되다 describes the result: being ready.

가다 → 갈 준비를 해요; 먹다 → 먹을 준비를 해요; 자다 → 잘 준비를 해요. It works with endings you already know: commands (준비를 하세요), the progressive (준비를 하고 있어요), and the past (준비를 했어요).

A noun can also go straight before 준비: 시험 준비 (exam prep), 여행 준비 (trip prep). 준비를 하다 can also be written as one word, 준비하다.

examples.en: Get ready to go out.
I am getting ready to leave now.
Hurry and get ready for bed.
Yesterday I prepared for the exam.
My friends are getting ready for the party.
Did you get ready to go to school?
